newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya riot police seal parliament before budget.
newsitem.headline: Kenya riot police seal parliament before budget.

text.p: Kenyan riot police sealed off parliament and deployed in force at strategic points around the capital on Thursday to prevent a banned pro-reform demonstration on Budget day.

Dozens of police, armed with long wooden staves, shields and teargas canisters, ringed the parliament building where President Daniel arap Moi was due to hear Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi's 1997/98 budget speech starting about 2.30 p.m. (1130 GMT).
Helmeted police patrolled Nairobi's main commercial district and men of the anti-riot General Service Unit (GSU) stood guard at strategic points.
Police armed with rifles manned roadblocks on access roads into Nairobi.

The usually bustling centre of the city of three million was quiet with only a fraction of the normal pedestrian and vehicle traffic. Some city centre schools and offices were closed because of fears that pro-democracy campaigners would defy a government ban and stage a protest outside parliament.
"It is clear that we may be entering an unsettled period," the headmaster of one suburban private school wrote in a letter to parents.
"I feel, in the interests of safety, it is best to take a low profile and reduce travelling to a minimum," he added, cancelling a school trip to Nairobi's museum on Thursday.
Some shops were closed and their owners had removed displays from the windows, fearing a repeat of two days of looting after an opposition rally was forcibly dispersed by police on May 31.

Reform leaders under the coalition National Convention Assembly banner (NCA) said they would assemble at midday (0900 GMT) on Thursday to go to parliament and present MPs with copies of two NCA-sponsored constitutional reform bills.
Moi has agreed to relax a tough law restricting public assemblies but ruled out any more constitutional reforms until after general elections to be held this year.

Moi, 73 this year, has yet to announce the election date. He looks certain to extend his 19-year rule for another five years, both because of the existing electoral rules and the deep personal and ethnic splits within the opposition.
